interactions.label: A 45-year-old man has a blood pressure of 136/88 mmHg on repeated measurement. H

params.question: A 45-year-old man has a blood pressure of 136/88 mmHg on repeated measurement. How is this reading classified under the ACC/AHA 2017 guideline versus the JNC 7 system?

answers.text: Stage 1 hypertension under both classification systems

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Under JNC 7, hypertension begins at 140/90 mmHg. A reading of 136/88 falls below that threshold and is classified as pre-hypertension, not Stage 1.

answers.text: Stage 1 under ACC/AHA 2017; pre-hypertension under JNC 7

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. ACC/AHA 2017 defines Stage 1 as 130–139/80–89 mmHg, so 136/88 qualifies. JNC 7 sets hypertension at ≥140/90, placing this reading in the pre-hypertension range. Indian guidelines (IGH-IV) follow the JNC 7 threshold.

answers.text: Normal under ACC/AHA 2017; Stage 1 under JNC 7

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This reverses the two systems. ACC/AHA 2017 has the lower threshold (≥130/80), so it classifies 136/88 as hypertension — not normal. JNC 7 uses ≥140/90 as its cut-off.

answers.text: Pre-hypertension under both classification systems

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: ACC/AHA 2017 eliminated the pre-hypertension category. Any reading ≥130/80 mmHg is now classified as hypertension. Only JNC 7 uses the pre-hypertension label for 120–139/80–89.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: ACC/AHA 2017 lowered the hypertension threshold to ≥130/80 mmHg, while JNC 7 (and Indian guidelines) retain ≥140/90. The same reading of 136/88 is Stage 1 in one system and pre-hypertension in the other.
Well done. Always state which classification system you are citing — the same reading can fall into different categories depending on the guideline used.

params.question: Which of the following clinical features most strongly suggests a secondary cause of hypertension rather than primary (essential) hypertension?

answers.text: Gradual onset of hypertension in a 55-year-old with a positive family history

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A gradual onset after age 40 with a family history is the classic pattern for primary hypertension, which accounts for 90–95% of cases. This presentation does not warrant an extensive secondary workup.

answers.text: Body mass index of 33 with a sedentary lifestyle and high dietary sodium

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Obesity, inactivity, and excess sodium are modifiable risk factors for primary hypertension. They raise blood pressure through increased vascular resistance and volume overload, but do not point to a specific secondary cause.

answers.text: Blood pressure well controlled on a single antihypertensive agent

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Good response to monotherapy is typical of primary hypertension. Resistance to three or more drugs (including a diuretic) is the red flag that suggests a secondary cause.

answers.text: Spontaneous hypokalaemia in the absence of diuretic therapy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Unexplained hypokalaemia without diuretic use is a classic pointer to primary aldosteronism, where excess aldosterone drives potassium wasting. This is one of the most important red flags for a secondary cause.

overallFeedback.feedback: Spontaneous hypokalaemia without diuretic use is the strongest red flag here — it points to primary aldosteronism. Other red flags include onset under age 40, resistance to three or more drugs, and episodic headache with palpitations and sweating.

Exactly. The key red flags for secondary hypertension include age under 40, resistant hypertension, spontaneous hypokalaemia, episodic symptoms (pheochromocytoma), and an arm-leg blood pressure discrepancy (coarctation).

interactions.label: A patient presents with blood pressure of 210/130 mmHg, papilloedema on fundosco

params.question: A patient presents with blood pressure of 210/130 mmHg, papilloedema on fundoscopy, and a rising serum creatinine. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

answers.text: Oral amlodipine with outpatient follow-up in 48 hours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Oral agents and outpatient follow-up are appropriate for hypertensive urgency, where there is no end-organ damage. This patient has papilloedema and renal injury — that is an emergency requiring intravenous therapy.

answers.text: Sublingual nifedipine for rapid blood pressure reduction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Sublingual nifedipine causes unpredictable, precipitous falls in blood pressure that can trigger cerebral or myocardial ischaemia. It must be avoided entirely in hypertensive crises.

answers.text: Intravenous antihypertensive therapy with ICU admission

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Papilloedema and rising creatinine indicate acute end-organ damage, making this a hypertensive emergency. The target is to reduce mean arterial pressure by no more than 25% in the first hour, using IV agents such as labetalol or nicardipine.

answers.text: Repeat blood pressure measurement after 30 minutes of rest

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Rest and re-measurement are reasonable for an incidentally discovered elevated reading. This patient has active end-organ damage — delaying treatment risks irreversible harm.

overallFeedback.feedback: Papilloedema and rising creatinine mean active end-organ damage — this is a hypertensive emergency. It requires IV therapy in an ICU. Reduce mean arterial pressure by no more than 25% in the first hour to avoid cerebral ischaemia.

Well applied. The same blood pressure of 210/130 is an urgency without damage but an emergency with it. Always examine for papilloedema, encephalopathy, and rising creatinine before deciding your treatment approach.

params.question: A normal 12-lead ECG reliably excludes left ventricular hypertrophy in a hypertensive patient.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: The statement is false. ECG voltage criteria such as Sokolow-Lyon detect only about half of anatomical LVH. A normal ECG does not exclude cardiac target organ damage — echocardiography is needed when clinical suspicion is high.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. The Sokolow-Lyon voltage criterion detects only about 50% of anatomical LVH confirmed on echocardiography. When clinical suspicion is high, a normal ECG should prompt escalation to echocardiography rather than reassurance.

interactions.label: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and proteinuria has Stage 2 hypertension.

params.question: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and proteinuria has Stage 2 hypertension. Which first-line antihypertensive class is most appropriate for him?

answers.text: Thiazide-like diuretic (e.g. chlorthalidone)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Thiazides are an excellent first-line choice for uncomplicated hypertension. However, in a patient with diabetes and proteinuria, an ACE inhibitor or ARB provides superior renal protection by reducing intraglomerular pressure.

answers.text: Beta-blocker (e.g. metoprolol)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Beta-blockers are reserved for specific indications such as heart failure with reduced ejection fraction or post-myocardial infarction. They are not first-line for uncomplicated hypertension or diabetic nephropathy.

answers.text: ACE inhibitor or ARB (e.g. ramipril or telmisartan)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. ACE inhibitors and ARBs are the preferred class when diabetes with proteinuria, chronic kidney disease, or heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is present. They reduce proteinuria by lowering intraglomerular pressure via efferent arteriolar dilatation.

answers.text: Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (e.g. verapamil)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Dihydropyridine CCBs such as amlodipine suit elderly patients and isolated systolic hypertension. Non-dihydropyridines like verapamil must be avoided in heart failure and are not the optimal choice for diabetic proteinuria.

overallFeedback.feedback: In a diabetic patient with proteinuria, an ACE inhibitor or ARB is the first-line choice. These agents reduce intraglomerular pressure and slow the progression of diabetic nephropathy — a benefit the other classes do not provide to the same degree.
Well reasoned. ACE inhibitors and ARBs target the RAAS pathway and are the drug class of choice whenever diabetes with proteinuria, CKD, or heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is present.

interactions.label: A hypertensive patient's blood pressure remains uncontrolled despite being presc

params.question: A hypertensive patient's blood pressure remains uncontrolled despite being prescribed three antihypertensive agents including a diuretic. Before adding a fourth drug, what should you assess first?

answers.text: Order a renal artery Doppler to exclude renovascular disease

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Investigating for a secondary cause is appropriate once resistant hypertension is confirmed. However, non-adherence must be excluded first — it is the commonest reason blood pressure appears uncontrolled on multiple agents.

answers.text: Switch to a different combination of the same three drug classes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Changing agents within the same classes adds complexity without addressing the commonest cause of apparent treatment failure. Confirm the patient is actually taking the prescribed drugs before altering the regimen.

answers.text: Check medication adherence

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Non-adherence is the most frequent cause of apparently resistant hypertension. Ask non-judgementally — 'Many people find it difficult to remember tablets every day. Has that been a challenge for you?' — and review dispensing records before adding drugs.

answers.text: Increase the dose of all three current medications

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Dose escalation without confirming adherence may expose the patient to side effects unnecessarily. If the patient is not taking the current doses reliably, higher doses will not solve the problem.

overallFeedback.feedback: Non-adherence is the commonest cause of apparent treatment failure in hypertension. Before adding a fourth agent or investigating for secondary causes, confirm the patient is actually taking all three prescribed medications.
Exactly. Always verify adherence before escalating therapy. A non-judgemental approach and dispensing record review often reveal the true reason for apparently resistant hypertension.
